rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to elute all 10 compounds if possible and map the overall elution window without risking severe truncation. The wide phi range and moderate slope give a good first read on whether early peaks are unretained, late peaks require stronger elution, and where to focus later optimization.

All compounds eluted well within the gradient, so trim the window to the observed elution range to reduce run time while keeping all peaks in-gradient. This should test whether a narrower, better-targeted phi window preserves resolution and improves the time term enough to beat the current method.

The broad window at 20 min already gave perfect resolution, so now test a steeper gradient to cut run time and see how much the critical mid-run pairs depend on slope. If resolution stays acceptable, this should improve CRF by reducing the time penalty.

The 10 min gradient is fast but over-compresses the critical cluster around peaks 5–7, while 20 min fully resolves everything. An intermediate slope should recover most of that lost resolution with only a modest increase in run time, likely improving the CRF further.

The critical pair 6/7 improves strongly with shallower slope, and 14 min is already near-optimal on time with only one sub-1.5 pair left. Testing 16 min should show whether a small extra decrease in slope resolves that pair enough to push CRF closer to 1.0 without incurring a meaningful time penalty.

The optimum in slope appears to lie between 10 and 16 min, with 14 min best so far; testing 12 min brackets that region and defines the CRF peak more precisely. This will confirm whether 14 min is truly optimal at 40 C or whether a slightly steeper gradient gives a better tradeoff.

The critical 6/7 pair responds to slope, but 14 min at 40 C is still just shy of full resolution, suggesting temperature may provide the needed selectivity shift. A 5 C decrease should modestly increase retention and can reorder or spread a close pair while keeping run time low enough that the time term should remain negligible.

Lowering temperature worsened selectivity by shifting the critical overlap from 6/7 to 5/6, so probe the opposite direction. A 5 C increase may improve selectivity for the crowded 5–7 cluster while retaining the near-optimal 14 min gradient shape.

Temperature shifts made the crowded middle cluster worse, so stay at 40 C and refine slope around the 14–16 min optimum. An 18 min gradient tests whether a modestly shallower slope can preserve full resolution with only a small enough time penalty to surpass the current best.

At 14 min and 40 C all peaks elute well before the gradient ends, with the last peak corresponding to only about phi_e ~0.58, so the upper end of the window is likely unnecessarily high. Lowering phi1 slightly should reduce effective gradient steepness in the crowded middle region and may improve the 6/7 separation without adding enough retention to trigger a time penalty.

Reducing phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 improved the critical 6/7 pair while keeping the run comfortably short, so continue narrowing the upper window. This should further shallow the effective gradient where peaks 5–8 elute and may lift the last sub-1.5 pair to baseline resolution with little or no time penalty.

At phi1 0.90 and 14 min the method is very close to perfect with no time penalty, so a slightly steeper gradient is worth testing to see if run time can be reduced while keeping the critical 6/7 pair acceptably resolved. This directly probes whether the 0.90 window is more tolerant to shorter tG than the 0.95 window was.

The 0.90 upper bound improved selectivity at 14 min, but 12 min was too steep; moving to 16 min should test whether that same window can achieve full resolution with only a small time cost. This helps determine whether the local optimum is at 14 or slightly shallower when phi1 is tuned to 0.90.

With slope now near-optimal at phi1 0.90, a temperature check is still worthwhile because the critical 6/7 pair remains the only limiter. Testing 35 C at this tuned window can reveal whether the selectivity behavior seen at phi1 0.95 changes when the gradient is less steep in the elution region.

The lower-temperature test again worsened selectivity by collapsing peaks 5/6, so check the opposite direction at the tuned phi1 0.90 window to complete the temperature picture. If 45 C also degrades the central cluster, that will confirm 40 C as the local temperature optimum and let us focus remaining injections on fine window tuning.

Both temperature directions are clearly worse, so keep 40 C and continue tuning the gradient window. Since phi1 = 0.85 gave full resolution but a small time penalty, testing phi1 = 0.80 will show whether further narrowing can preserve or improve the critical mid-cluster spacing enough to offset the likely retention increase.

The optimum appears centered near phi1 = 0.90 and 40 C, so now test whether raising phi0 slightly improves use of the gradient window without sacrificing selectivity. The first peak is not near dead time, but trimming unused low-organic range could mildly reshape the crowded middle region and reduce overall retention enough to improve CRF.

Raising phi0 to 0.10 improved both run time and the critical cluster, making this the new best region; now test a slightly narrower upper bound around that optimum. If phi1 = 0.85 keeps the strengthened 6/7 separation while avoiding added time penalty, it could reach the maximum CRF.

We have already reached the maximum CRF, so the main goal now is to confirm the optimum neighborhood and learn whether the score plateau extends to a slightly narrower window. Testing phi1 = 0.80 from the winning phi0/tG/T settings checks robustness while staying close to the established optimum.

Since narrowing phi1 below 0.85 hurt only through time, probe the other edge of the winning window by increasing phi0 further. This tests whether the low-organic segment is still wider than needed and whether a slightly higher starting composition can keep full resolution while shortening the run enough to stay on the CRF maximum plateau.

We are on the CRF maximum plateau, so continue mapping its boundary by raising phi0 one more step from another winning method. This checks how far the start composition can be increased before the earliest peak becomes effectively too weakly retained or the critical pair begins to compress.

The maximum plateau includes phi0 = 0.15 with phi1 = 0.85, and phi1 = 0.90 performed well at lower phi0, so this run maps the neighboring corner of that plateau. It tests whether a slightly wider upper window at the improved start composition preserves full resolution while keeping the time term at zero.

With the optimum plateau located, use a remaining run to probe whether the winning window tolerates a shorter gradient. This tests if phi0 0.10/phi1 0.85 can reduce analysis time further while still keeping the critical 6/7 pair above the resolution threshold.

One winning composition set remains untested at shorter tG, and its higher phi0 may tolerate compression slightly better than the 0.10 start. This run checks whether the second CRF-max plateau point can retain perfect scoring at 12 min or confirms 14 min as the shortest robust optimum.

For the final run, map the last nearby corner of the optimum region by combining the successful higher phi0 with a lower phi1. This will confirm whether the CRF maximum plateau is centered specifically at phi1 = 0.85 or extends further downward when phi0 is 0.15.
